newsitem.title: USA: Bringing Bible stories to life for children.
newsitem.headline: Bringing Bible stories to life for children.

text.p: I'll admit to some trepidation when it came to looking at "The Story of Creation" (Little Ark Interactive, Windows/Macintosh, $20) a CD-ROM storybook for ages 3 to 7.

After all, the Genesis account of creation has been an source of rancour between Christians who believe the Bible's version and scientists who have determined that Earth and its creatures have developed and evolved over the past 4.5 billion years.

Not to worry. This adaptation of the first two chapters of Genesis is a delight. Superior to most CD-ROM children's books, "The Story of Creation" has a simple story (it stops before you get to the snake and the apple), fine music and sound effects, and a child narrator whose enthusiasm is truly infectious.

Youngsters can have the story read to them, which takes 8-1/2 minutes, or they can go through the tale at their own pace, clicking on various objects to make them come alive. A palm tree, for example, turns into a hula dancer.

Little Ark also has come out with "Daniel in the Lion's Den" for the same price. Narrated by a cat, it features three wise guys who act a bit like Moe, Larry and Curly, and who plot to turn Daniel, the devout Jew, into feline fodder by getting the king to pass a law that imposes the death sentence on anyone caught praying to God.

Needless to say, Daniel's faith earns him a guardian angel, who keeps the lions at bay. As an added bonus, it features a guest appearance by a surprisingly-affectionate Loch Ness Monster. It lasts nearly 14 minutes.
They may not win awards for historical accuracy, but "The Story of Creation" and "Daniel in the Lion's Den" tell engaging stories are perfectly tailored to this age group.

"Compton's Interactive Bible: New International Version" (Compton's New Media, Windows, $50) allows you to quickly search for passages, pictures and even music, and comes with a free disk of 24 "Children's Bible Stories" for ages 3 to 8.

These stories, which cover both the Old and New Testament, have a much more traditional style than the Little Ark series. The narration is uninspired. God -- surprise, surprise -- has a deep voice with plenty of reverb thrown in to make him sound imposing.

While the Little Ark stories automatically play from beginning to end, a child using the Compton's stories must click on a button to go on to each page. There are no animated objects in the story to click on. The only thing a child can activate is some cartoon animals who mouth platitudes that have little to do with the story.

However, for the price you'd pay for two or three Little Ark stories, you can get two dozen Compton's stories, plus the computerized Bible, which is a handy tool in itself. It lets you search for Bible passages, shows you Bible-inspired works of art, offers videos on various topics, lets you compare the Gospels (albeit, with some difficulty) and provides expert commentary.

For example, the "Interactive Bible" explains how Mark's simple, succinct and unadorned version was probably used as a basis for Matthew's version, which was written in Greek for a largely-Jewish audience and which bends over backwards to show how the life of Jesus was a fulfilment of Old Testament prophesy.

"Compton's Interactive Bible" is a handy resource for adults, and for children whose interest in the Bible has matured beyond the stories to the point where they are ready to learn about the culture, traditions, and myths that have shaped the book that shaped Western culture.
Some new and notable software in the stores this week:

"The Atomic Files" (L3 Interactive, Windows, $35) -- A multimedia look at the the Nuclear Age and the impact it has had on the world. It includes a history of the Manhattan Project, interviews with Edward Teller (the father of the hydrogen bomb) and Hiroshima survivor Kaz Suyeishi, World War II propaganda campaigns and an exploration of how wartime fever played out in movies, radio, comics and music.

"Koala Lumpur: Journey to the Edge" (Broderbund, Windows, $39) -- Billed as "a comic adventure with an attitude," players must prevent impending doom by joining forces with Dr. Dingo Tu Far and finding the Lost Scroll of Cartoon Prophesies. The offbeat characters include a shady ventriloquist dummy.

"Krazy Ivan" (Psygnosis, Windows95, $50) -- A "Mech Warrior"-style game in which players control a 40-foot-high Soviet soldier who has to battle more than 30 different types of robots in five different battle zones. The developer says this game has more tongue-in-cheek elements, including a "Schitzo" mode, which briefly reverses the player's controls.

"Valhalla" (Access Software, Windows/Macintosh, $25) lets you simulate playing golf at the Valhalla Golf Club in Louisville, Kentucky, where last year's PGA championship was played. It can only be used by people who already have a version of "Links" or "Microsoft Golf."
(Gene Emery is a columnist who covers science and technology. His Internet address is gene.emery(at)prodigy.com. Any opinions in the column are his alone.)
